print('metadata',r.metadata)
for i,p in enumerate(r.pages):
 text=p.extract_text(extraction_mode='layout')
 Path(f'tmp/pdfs/page-{i+1:02}.txt').write_text(text)
 print(f'PAGE {i+1}: {len(text)} chars')
Path('tmp/pdfs/manuscript.txt').write_text('\\n\\n'.join(f'=== PAGE {i+1} ===\\n'+p.extract_text(extraction_mode='layout') for i,p in enumerate(r.pages)))
PY"

strengths: The virtual-correspondence approach provides a useful methodological simplification of the difficult 4p3v problem by reusing established five-point and P3P solvers. Its simplicity and demonstrated competitive behavior provide the principal case for weak acceptance.

Table 1 supports competitive accuracy against the dedicated homotopy solver: 4p3v(M) achieves AUC@5 of 42.71 versus 43.25 on Sacre Coeur and 18.35 versus 19.45 on St. Peter’s Square, without requiring a learned model. The learned variant improves these scores to 47.14 and 21.34 despite training exclusively on synthetic data.

The evaluation combines 10,000 real image triplets, controlled noise experiments, a substantial centroid-correspondence study, oracle comparisons, and a two-view extension evaluated on 9,900 pairs. Including the strong 5pt+P3P baseline and acknowledging its favorable performance makes the empirical comparison useful beyond the proposed methods.

The manuscript clearly explains the distinction between the overconstrained four-triplet configuration and the genuinely minimal mixed-visibility configuration. It acknowledges approximation errors and two-view underdetermination. The centroid method is straightforward to implement, and the supplement supplies substantial network and training details.
weaknesses: The practical accuracy–runtime advantage is limited. In Table 1, 4p3v(L) takes 14.13–38.50 seconds per triplet versus 2.46–2.59 seconds for 5pt+P3P, while generally delivering similar or slightly worse accuracy. The centroid variant is also slower than the homotopy baseline on both scenes. The strongest demonstrated benefit is implementation simplicity; the learned variant has a substantial efficiency limitation.

The evaluation does not fully validate three-camera geometry. Section 5 measures rotations and translation directions for pairs 1–2 and 1–3, and its Sampson scoring uses the same pairs. These quantities are insensitive to the relative baseline scale ||t13||/||t12||, which is part of the three-camera reconstruction. Baseline-ratio or jointly aligned camera-center errors would be needed to assess this missing component.

The approximation’s reliability is insufficiently characterized. The triangle-based bound in Section 3.3 can be large, and Figures 3–4 show appreciable errors even without image noise. The manuscript does not establish how these errors vary with depth variation, viewing obliquity, or triangle extent, leaving the favorable operating regime unclear.

The large number of test triplets comes from only two landmark scenes. More consequentially, the anticipated advantage under high outlier contamination is not tested through an outlier-rate sweep or accuracy-versus-time comparison. Table 3 supports a preliminary two-view extension, but broader applicability to other camera-geometry problems remains conjectural.

Experimental reproducibility remains incomplete: RANSAC thresholds, stopping budgets, local-optimization details, and handling of multiple solver solutions are insufficiently specified, while implementation availability is only promised. A smaller clarity issue is the permutation-invariance claim in Section 3.2: choosing the first two points for normalization and the first three for the centroid makes the complete preprocessing pipeline order-dependent unless an additional canonicalization is used.
